Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate the ellipse shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, $a=2$ and $b=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224904/assets/7540559d86e836d869173da11ca0f7befba8ead07c844be1c9708591fb372042.png)

The quarter-ellipse above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +h,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +k,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(3,1),$ $a=2$ and $b=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse and the line parallel to the $x$-axis and crossing the center of the ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224904/assets/30bb7c769ff0cbabcb13e3f48aaad1e4c8c34ded6b571858248eb9819eb2bbe4.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$, we get the quarter-ellipse.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-ellipse are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{3}{2}x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{9}{4}{x}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{y}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}{y}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}{y}^{2}=1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $3$ and vertical radius $1,$ as shown below. Which set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(3,0)?$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224904/assets/5d791b30556f41973c8f1a9b8702744afae72458d0ce285de2b7ef8fa19d720a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x= a\cos\theta,\quad y=b\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(a,0).$

In our case, $a=3$ and $b=1.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x= 3\cos\theta,\quad y=\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

x= a\cos\theta+h,\quad y=b\sin\theta+k, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).

The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x= a\cos\theta,\quad y=b\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, $a=5$ and $b=4.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x= 5\cos\theta,\quad y=4\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a semi-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224904/assets/a64898381b2cf50c71a79a3dbcf02b9a83f320b8c2d1ba542b3beecc05e17625.png)

$$

$$

Example: 
                    The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x= 4\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta - 1, \quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{4} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y+1}{2} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1.
$$
